title: Chapter 80 — The Nut
paragraphs: If the Sperm Whale is physiognomically a Sphinx, to the phrenologist his brain seems that geometrical circle which it is impossible to square.

In the full-grown creature, the skull will measure at least twenty feet in length. Unhinge the lower jaw, and the side view of this skull is like a moderately inclined plane resting throughout on a level base. But in life — as we have seen elsewhere — this inclined plane is filled up to the front, and this vast mass forms the forehead of the whale. Lift the skull from behind, and you expose the brain.

It is plain, then, that phrenologically the head of this Leviathan, in the creature's living state, is an entire delusion. As for his true brain, you can see no indication of it, nor feel any. The whale, like all things that are mighty, wears a false brow before the common world.

If you unload his skull of its spermaceti heaps and then take a rear view of the back end, which is the high end, you will be struck by its resemblance to the human skull, seen from the same angle and the same point of view. Indeed, place this reversed skull — scaled down to human size — among a collection of skulls, and you would involuntarily confuse it with them. And the resemblance goes deeper. In both the whale and the human, the spine enters at the rear, slightly below the top.

But if from the comparatively small dimensions of the whale's actual brain you deem it incapable of being adequately studied, then I have another idea for you. If you carefully examine almost any four-legged animal's spine, you will be struck by the resemblance of its vertebrae to a string of dwarfed skulls. The base of the human skull is like the first vertebra, and the vertebra like the skull in miniature. So, in the spinal cord of the whale there runs a succession of these connected skull-like shapes.

Apply this spinal branch of phrenology to the Sperm Whale. His brain-cavity is continuous with the first neck-vertebra. And in that vertebra the bottom of the spinal canal will measure ten inches across, being eight in height, and of a triangular shape with the base downward. As it passes through the remaining vertebrae, the canal tapers in size but maintains its proportions.

But leaving this hint to work as it may with the phrenologists, I would merely assume the spinal theory for a moment, in reference to the Sperm Whale's hump. This noble hump, if I am not mistaken, rises over one of the larger vertebrae, and is therefore, in some way, the outer convex mold of it. From its relative position, then, I should call this high hump the organ of firmness or indomitableness in the Sperm Whale. And that he possesses this quality in remarkable degree — all who know him will acknowledge.
